title: Getting around Budapest: a first-visit transport guide
description: Understand Budapest public transport, single-ticket validation, travelcards, BudapestGO and the special ticket for the 100E Airport Express.

heroImage.alt: A yellow Budapest tram crossing the green iron Liberty Bridge

intro: Start with the places you want to visit, then choose transport that fits your day. Walking works well for compact sightseeing stops; metro, tram and bus connections help you cover the gaps. The main thing to get right is the ticket you hold and how it must be used.
highlights: 100E Airport Express uses a special fare

sections.title: Group your stops before choosing transport

children.text: Put nearby sights together: one outing for Castle Hill, another for downtown Pest and a separate block for City Park. This avoids turning each attraction into a cross-city journey. Start and finish with the address of your accommodation, not just the neighbourhood name.

For your first day, keep one simple route saved and leave time to find the stop or platform. Use BKK’s current journey information when you travel; this guide does not provide live routing or disruption notices.

sections.title: Buying a single ticket is not the last step

children.text: BKK explains that single tickets need validation when you start travelling. Paper tickets use a validator; digital tickets follow the scanning instructions in BudapestGO. Keep the validated ticket available throughout the journey.

A regular single ticket generally covers one uninterrupted ride, with a metro-transfer exception when continuing in the same direction. For a journey involving other transfers, compare time-based tickets or a travelcard instead of assuming one single ticket covers everything.

sections.title: Single tickets, timed tickets or a travelcard?

children.text: Think about your actual pattern: two journeys surrounding a long walking day are different from repeatedly crossing between districts. Check the products currently offered by BKK, then compare the options for your intended journeys.

BKK’s 30- and 90-minute digital tickets allow transfers within their rules, but require scanning when you change vehicles. Daily travelcards allow unlimited transfers within their validity and do not require single-ticket-style validation. Read the current product conditions before buying.

sections.title: Airport journeys: check the 100E fare separately

children.text: The airport describes 100E Airport Express as a direct connection between Liszt Ferenc Airport and Deák Ferenc tér in central Pest. It requires a special ticket, so do not assume your regular city single ticket covers the airport journey.

Choose a route from the airport to your actual accommodation and reverse that check before departure. Allow for luggage, walking to your stop and check-in requirements. Current airport stopping patterns and timetables should come from the operator, not a fixed travel-time promise in a guide.

sections.title: Small habits that make the day easier

children.text: Save your hotel address and an offline note of the route back. Keep your phone charged if your ticket is digital, and check what you must show during inspection. For accessibility needs, examine the specific service and stop rather than assuming every connection is step-free.

Use official BKK sales channels and check the fare there before purchasing. As an editorial suggestion, leave a little flexibility in your first journey instead of booking a timed attraction immediately after arrival.
Check your route shortly before leaving.
Read ticket conditions before payment.
Keep tickets and booking confirmations within easy reach.

sections.title: Metro lines and the HÉV suburban railway

children.text: Budapest has four metro lines, M1 to M4. M1, the Millennium Underground Railway, is the oldest: it opened in 1896, runs under Andrássy út between Vörösmarty tér and Mexikói út, and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site that covers the Danube banks, the Buda Castle quarter and Andrássy Avenue. Its stops include Opera, Oktogon, Hősök tere and Széchenyi fürdő, so it links the downtown with City Park. BKK confirms that single tickets and passes work on it, and that you validate before you enter the platform area.

The other lines are M2 (Déli pályaudvar to Örs vezér tere), M3 (Újpest-központ to Kőbánya-Kispest) and M4 (Keleti pályaudvar to Kelenföld vasútállomás), which opened in 2014 and runs without drivers. Deák Ferenc tér is the transfer point for M1, M2 and M3. The HÉV is the suburban railway; its lines carry the numbers H5 to H9. Inside the Budapest boundary a normal BKK ticket or travelcard is valid on the HÉV, but a trip beyond it needs a suburban ticket. MÁV names the boundary stations as Békásmegyer (H5), Millenniumtelep (H6), Ilonatelep (H8) and Szabadságtelep (H9), and notes that H7 lies entirely within Budapest.

sections.title: Trams, buses and the night network

children.text: Trams do much of the sightseeing work. A 2017 guide from We Love Budapest describes tram 2 as running along the Pest embankment past the Great Market Hall, the Palace of Arts, the Chain Bridge and Parliament towards Jászai Mari tér. Trams 4 and 6 follow the Grand Boulevard, the semicircle that links Margaret Bridge and Petőfi Bridge through Pest, and reach Buda at Széll Kálmán tér in the north and Újbuda-központ (line 4) or Móricz Zsigmond körtér (line 6) in the south. Track works change these routes from time to time, as the 2025 Grand Boulevard renovation did, so confirm the current route in BudapestGO before you rely on a line.

On Castle Hill buses fill the gap: BKK lists buses 16, 16A and 116 at the upper funicular station, and trams 19 and 41 and buses 16 and 105 at the lower one. Trolleybuses also exist; BKK mentions lines 70, 78 and 79. At night BKK's night-transport page says tram 6 runs around the clock and names the 100E and 200E airport buses and numerous night bus services. The same page says the night network was reorganised from the night of 1 and 2 July 2026 and describes the metro as running extended hours rather than all night, so plan a late journey in advance instead of assuming the metro will carry you home.
Use the stop name, not only the line number, when checking a route.
Tram 6 is the one tram BKK describes as running around the clock.

sections.title: Funicular, chairlift, heritage trams and boats

children.text: BKK groups several scenic services as special transport, and they follow their own ticket rules. The Buda Castle Funicular, in service since 1870, links Clark Ádám tér at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge with Szent György tér beside the palace. Only a funicular ticket is valid there, sold at its ticket offices and other designated locations or as an e-ticket, and BKK tickets and passes are not accepted. You validate at the machine as you cross the platform boundary and keep the ticket until you leave the station area.

The Zugliget Chairlift (Libegő) climbs towards János-hegy in the Buda Hills when the weather permits and also needs its own ticket. Historic trams, trolleybuses and buses run from spring to autumn on heritage services that need a heritage ticket or travelcard. The cogwheel railway accepts regular BKK fares, but early and late trips run on demand and must be requested in advance. Among boats, BKK describes the D14 ferry between Csepel-Királyerdő and Soroksár, Molnár-sziget, a local crossing rather than a sightseeing route. BKK adds that BKV runs its tourist boats separately, so do not assume a BKK ticket covers a sightseeing cruise.

sections.title: Walk or ride, and what to know about access

children.text: Treat these as editorial suggestions rather than measured times. Near the Chain Bridge the funicular's lower station is right at the Buda bridgehead, so one short ride or a climb up the hill are both realistic, and the funicular needs its own ticket. For Andrássy Avenue, City Park and Széchenyi, M1 stops at Opera, Oktogon, Hősök tere and Széchenyi fürdő, so riding one way and strolling the other works well. Along the river, tram 2 passes the Great Market Hall and Parliament, which makes it useful for linking riverside sights, but the Danube bank itself is also a walking route.

BKK's accessibility page gives specifics. All M4 stations are accessible by lift. On M2 only Örs vezér tere, Pillangó utca and Puskás Ferenc Stadion are step-free, and BKK says its deep-level stations were not made accessible. On M3 the reconstructed stations have lifts and inclines. BKK says stops on tram lines 1, 3, 4 and 6 are barrier-free, except Boráros tér on line 6. Over 90 percent of buses are low-floor, and trams are low-floor on roughly 30 percent of lines. In the BudapestGO planner you can tap a vehicle icon to learn whether it is low-floor. For any other station or stop, check before you travel.

Ticket inspection is a real part of using the network. BKK states that anyone without a valid ticket, pass or travel document must pay a penalty fare, and that settling it later costs more. On the metro the row of validators also marks the platform boundary: BKK warns that if you cross it without a ticket, or with a non-validated one, you can already be fined. If a validator is broken, use another nearby, and if you are moved to a replacement vehicle, punch the other end of your validated paper ticket.

The mistakes that follow from this are easy to avoid. Do not forget to validate a paper single ticket. Do not use a regular single ticket on the 100E, which BKK says it does not cover. Do not expect a BKK pass on the funicular, chairlift or a tourist boat. Do not take the HÉV beyond the city boundary on a Budapest-only ticket; MÁV says the Budapest pass is only valid on the Budapest sections. Finally, do not treat an old blog's route or station detail as current: check BudapestGO or the BKK pages on the day you travel.

faqs.question: Can I use a regular single ticket on the 100E?
faqs.answer: No. BKK states that regular single tickets are not valid on 100E Airport Express. Check the current airport-ticket options directly with BKK.

faqs.question: Do daily travelcards need single-ticket validation?
faqs.answer: BKK says daily travelcards and passes do not require validation. Follow any instructions to show the ticket or pass, and use it within its validity.

faqs.question: Does the metro run through the night?
faqs.answer: BKK's night-transport page does not describe overnight metro service. It says tram 6 runs around the clock, names the 100E and 200E airport buses and numerous night bus services, and says the night network was reorganised from the night of 1 and 2 July 2026. Plan a late return in advance in BudapestGO.

faqs.question: Can I use my BKK ticket or travelcard on the Buda Castle Funicular?
faqs.answer: No. BKK says only a funicular ticket, sold at the funicular ticket offices, other designated locations or as an e-ticket, is valid there. Other BKK tickets and passes do not apply, and the ticket has to be validated at the machine.

faqs.question: Do I need a different ticket for the HÉV outside Budapest?
faqs.answer: Yes. Within Budapest a normal BKK ticket or travelcard works on the HÉV, but MÁV says a HÉV ticket is valid only on the suburban sections and that the Budapest pass is only valid on the Budapest sections. Check the boundary stations for your line before you travel.

faqs.question: Is Budapest public transport step-free?
faqs.answer: Only partly. BKK says all M4 stations have lifts, only three M2 stations are step-free, and the reconstructed M3 stations are accessible. It lists tram lines 1, 3, 4 and 6 as barrier-free stops, with the Boráros tér stop of line 6 excepted. Check the specific stop before you go.

title: Buda Castle District: a self-guided first visit
description: Plan a self-guided Castle District visit around Fisherman’s Bastion, Matthias Church, Trinity Square and time to wander.

heroImage.alt: The white conical towers and terraces of Fisherman's Bastion with the Buda hills behind

intro: The Castle District is most rewarding when you give it more than a photo stop. Start with its familiar landmarks, then leave room for the streets between them. This is a suggested walking sequence, not a timed tour: adjust the distance and number of interiors to your own pace.
highlights: Separate the Bastion’s lower and upper-level access
Leave space for a quieter stretch of the district

children.text: Castle Hill deserves a little arrival planning. Check a current BKK route from your accommodation and decide whether you want to walk up or reduce the climb. For anyone with mobility needs, review the approach and venue access independently; a viewpoint being nearby does not mean the route is step-free.

Our suggestion is to reserve a half-day if you want a mix of streets, viewpoints and an interior visit. That is an editorial allowance, not an official tour duration. If you have only a short window, focus on one part of the district rather than rushing across it.

sections.title: Begin at Trinity Square and Matthias Church

children.text: Use Trinity Square as an orientation point. The district’s official visitor guide groups Matthias Church, Fisherman’s Bastion and the Holy Trinity Column around this square, which makes it a useful place to start your visit.

Pause to take in the church exterior before choosing whether to go inside. Check the church’s own website for the visitor schedule and tickets on your date. Do not build a tightly timed route around opening hours copied from an old article or a search snippet.

sections.title: Fisherman’s Bastion: understand the two levels

children.text: Visit Budavár lists the lower level as free and the upper lookout as paid. Explore the lower terraces and take in the view across to Pest before deciding whether you want the additional upper-level access.

Give yourself time to look beyond a single photo angle. Consider a later walk along the Buda riverbank as a second perspective on the same cityscape. This is a suggestion for variety, not a promise of a particular sunset, weather or crowd level.

sections.title: Leave the main viewpoints behind for a while

children.text: Continue to Tóth Árpád Promenade for a change of outlook. The district visitor guide describes a walk along the castle wall with views towards the Buda hills. It offers a different direction to look after spending time facing the Danube.

Choose a manageable loop and pause before adding another major stop. If you continue towards the palace area, treat any museum interior as a separate decision with its own opening hours and tickets. You can enjoy the neighbourhood without trying to enter every building.

Keep the return journey flexible. You might spend more time in the district, continue towards the river or use a current public-transport connection back to Pest. Check your onward route before committing to a long downhill walk.

Wear shoes you are comfortable walking in and leave space for rests. In poor weather, shorten the outdoor route rather than trying to keep every viewpoint. A slower visit with fewer stops is still a complete Castle District experience.
Check church access on your date.
Treat each paid attraction separately.
Plan the approach and return around your mobility needs.

sections.title: Castle Hill in a few dates

children.text: The first royal residence on Castle Hill was built between 1247 and 1265 under Béla IV. Matthias Corvinus rebuilt the palace in an early Renaissance style after his marriage to Beatrice of Naples in 1476. Buda fell to the Ottomans in 1541, and the siege that ended Ottoman rule in 1686 destroyed the medieval palace. A Baroque palace was finished in 1769, the Royal Palace was officially inaugurated in 1912, and the siege of 1944–45 left it in ruins before the post-war reconstruction of 1952–1966. The Castle Quarter was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987.

Two small stops reward a detour. The Vienna Gate at the northern end of the district was rebuilt in 1936, to a design by Jenő Kismarty-Lechner, to mark the 250th anniversary of the recapture of Buda. And at the bottom of the hill, at Clark Ádám tér beside the Chain Bridge, stands the Zero Kilometre Stone, a three-metre limestone sculpture by Miklós Borsos erected in 1975.

sections.title: Getting up the hill and moving around

children.text: The Buda Castle Funicular links Clark Ádám tér, at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, with Szent György tér beside the palace. BKK’s page says the track is 95 metres long and climbs about 50 metres, and that BKV Zrt. operates it. It opened in 1870, was wrecked in the Second World War and returned to service in 1986. Regular BKK travel passes are not valid on it, but a Budapest Card Plus is, and the page lists scheduled maintenance days. If you walk instead, the visitor site says pedestrian routes, stairways and ramps lead up the hill.

Expect cobblestones, stairs and slopes, and wear sturdy shoes. Visit Budavár says several parts are accessible, or reachable with a companion, but the historic setting has steeper stretches; its map marks easier and more demanding sections. It suggests mornings or late afternoons for a quieter visit and museums as the indoor alternative in bad weather. People live here: stay on the routes, keep noise down and do not enter residential doorways or courtyards.

sections.title: Behind the walls: the palace and the museums underground

children.text: The Royal Palace is a cultural centre rather than one attraction. Visit Budavár lists the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum’s Castle Museum and the National Széchényi Library as its occupants. The National Gallery was founded in 1957 and shows Hungarian art from the Middle Ages to the twentieth century; its own site notes that the dome and crypt have separate access conditions. Choose one museum and treat it as its own visit.

Under the hill, the Hospital in the Rock was built from 1941 to 1943 by enlarging cave tunnels and opened in February 1944. It treated civilians and soldiers during the siege, reopened in the 1956 revolution, and was converted into a nuclear bunker between 1958 and 1962. Wikipedia says entry is by guided tour only, and the museum’s site mentions English tours with audio guides. Visit Budavár also lists a separate Buda Castle Labyrinth, a cave and cellar system beneath the hill.

sections.title: Matthias Church and the Bastion: what you are looking at

children.text: Matthias Church is older than it looks. Béla IV replaced an earlier church with a three-nave basilica between 1255 and 1269, and Matthias Corvinus added the southwest bell tower and married Beatrice of Naples there in 1476. From 1541 until 1686 it served as Buda’s main mosque, and Franz Joseph I was crowned in it in 1867. The Holy Trinity Column in front is a plague memorial erected in 1713.

Fisherman’s Bastion is much younger than it looks. Frigyes Schulek built it between 1895 and 1902 in a neo-Romanesque style, and its seven towers symbolise the seven chieftains of the Hungarians who founded the country in 895. The equestrian statue of King Stephen I between the Bastion and the church, by Alajos Stróbl, was erected in 1906. The name probably comes from the Danube-side settlement of Fishtown, or from a wall section entrusted to the fishermen’s guild.

faqs.question: Do I need one ticket for the whole Castle District?
faqs.answer: No single ticket is required simply to explore the neighbourhood’s public streets. Individual venues and paid lookout areas have their own admission arrangements.

faqs.question: How long should I allow?
faqs.answer: Our suggested allowance is a half-day for unhurried wandering and an optional interior. Adapt that to your mobility, interests and any confirmed entry times.

faqs.question: Can I use a regular BKK pass on the Castle Hill funicular?
faqs.answer: BKK’s funicular page says regular BKK travel passes are not valid on it, while a Budapest Card Plus gives free return trips. BKV Zrt. operates the line, so check its page for current ticket options and scheduled maintenance days.

faqs.question: Is the Castle District suitable with a stroller or limited mobility?
faqs.answer: Visit Budavár says several parts are accessible or reachable with a companion and the main squares are reasonably stroller-friendly, but cobblestones, stairs and slopes are common. Its map marks easier and more demanding sections, so plan your route from it.

faqs.question: What is the Hospital in the Rock?
faqs.answer: It is a museum in the cave tunnels beneath Castle Hill, built as an emergency hospital in the early 1940s and later converted into a nuclear bunker. Wikipedia says access is limited to guided tours, so check the museum’s own site for how visits are arranged.
